generatedProse.concept-context: In psychology, marking criteria make the standard explicit for essays, lab reports and reviews. They usually judge knowledge and understanding of theory and evidence, the clarity and structure of your writing and referencing, and your critical evaluation of studies rather than mere description. Reading your own draft against those dimensions, before you submit, is how psychology students stop guessing what a strong report looks like.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students apply the same marking criteria to their own lab report before submitting.

Tom reads the report through, feels it is fine, and submits. Asked which band it meets on critical evaluation, Tom cannot say: the report describes the studies well but does not weigh their methods. Tom judged the work by effort and length, not against the criteria, and so missed that it sat a band lower than hoped.

Amara reads the report against each dimension in turn. Knowledge of the theory: strong. Communication: clear, though the results section wanders. Critical evaluation: thin, mostly description of the studies. Amara can name the band each dimension meets and why, and revises the evaluation before submitting. The judgement is reasoned and tied to the criteria.

Both had the same criteria. Only Amara applied them, and turned the appraisal into a better report.
generatedProse.summary: Marking criteria in psychology set out the standard your essays and reports are judged against, by dimension and level. Applying them to your own draft is self-assessment: you read as a marker would, name the band each dimension meets, and revise where it falls short. You can now appraise a piece of work against criteria and justify the judgement. The next lesson does the same for the feedback you receive.

check.body: In the worked example, what let Amara justify the grade her report would earn?

items.text: She appraised the report against each dimension of the criteria and could say which band it met and why.
She wrote more than Tom did.
She submitted the report earlier than Tom did.
She preferred her own work to Tom's.

feedback.correct: That's right. Judging each dimension against the criteria is what makes the judgement justifiable.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for how Amara tied the judgement to the criteria.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara could justify the grade because she appraised the report against each dimension and named the band it met. Length, timing or preference do not justify a judgement.
